    "description": "Jacob Kimmel thinks he can find the transcription factors to reverse aging. We do a deep dive on why this might be plausible and why evolution hasn’t already optimized for longevity. We also talk about why drug discovery has been getting exponentially harder, and what a new platform for biological understanding to speed up progress would look like. As a bonus, we get into the nitty gritty of gene delivery and Jacob’s controversial takes on CAR-T cells. For full disclosure, I am an angel investor in NewLimit. This did not impact my decision to interview Jacob, nor the questions I asked him.\n\n𝐄𝐏𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐃𝐄 𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐊𝐒\n* Transcript: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/jacob-kimmel\n* Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/why-evolution-designed-us-to-die-fast-how-we-can-change/id1516093381?i=1000722975425\n* Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/episode/3xUwUYLpjGI3bxsEM114jq?si=mo4FBuI4RoG42PUYYCFUDw\n\n𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐍𝐒𝐎𝐑𝐒\n* Hudson River Trading uses deep learning to tackle one of the world's most complex systems: global capital allocation. They have a massive in-house GPU cluster, and they’re constantly adding new racks of B200s to ensure their researchers are never constrained by compute. Explore opportunities at https://hudsonrivertrading.com/dwarkesh\n\n* Google’s Gemini CLI turns ideas into working applications FAST, no coding required. It built a complete podcast post-production tool in 10 minutes, including fully functional backend logic, and the entire build used less than 10% of Gemini’s session context.       "text": "6:06 This could actually be the explanation. From 25-30 our cerebral cortex has just finished developing and have just enough data (life experience/knowledge) to generalize well.       "parent": "UgzdxQDF2HCBYBbUZ114AaABAg",
      "text": "Yes and no, aging is more complex than just the shortening of telomeres and telomeres only shorten because they act as a cancer suppression system, if they didn't shorten the likelihood of cancer would increase dramatically and immune systems and cells would still weaken with age from cell replication errors, cell damage from radiation/oxidative stress, immune compromises etc. so a species of organism without the shortening would likely die out very fast. Red blood cells don't reproduce (They are produced from stem cells) and die after around 120 days this is because they are terminally differentiated to maximize the surface area (oxygen transportation) capabilities, if these cells didn't die they would circulate around the body and become damaged to the point of anemia and would starve organs from their oxygen supply and you would die.\n\nThis isn't exactly accurate because red blood cells are recycled by phagocytes which recycle the damaged/dead blood cells rather telomere shortening but again imagine if the vast majority of these phagocytes in the body were cancerous/unable to perform this function and the consequences are the same.\n\nIn short, telomeres that shorten paradoxically extend the life of organisms like mammals across the species because high turnover cells don't become cancerous and kill you. Also I don't think self-repairing is possible without cell death ironically for the same reasons. It's like how to clean something you have to make something else dirty or in this case for the organism to stay alive cells have to die.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCsz1LPqMnf7LG4bzIRCOf6g",

      "text": "They talk about gene’s updating to solve problems like the genes are figuring out sudoku puzzles… I have yet to see one notable gene mutation that has fixed any of humanities problems… And we have far more people alive today than we’ve ever had in the history of mankind.\n\nWe probably only had a few thousand humans alive when we supposedly had all of these novel mutations that were solutions.. and now with 8 billion there are none.",

      "text": "This is one of the best explanations of this topic I've ever watched.       "id": "UgybEXi64ibVeKUZOyZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The exceptions to rate of living theory of aging were found to be due to difference in membrane composition.   Gene changesmaking membranes less susceptible to damage are among the most strongly selected in longevous organisms.",

      "author_id": "UCucqd0Q8S1cibjXurG_Q6kg",
      "author": "@diamond_s",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m12INDxrehfzOzq9xofITYAuYy19N2eCjpk5y_Rbnv8Q=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "Ugxy-Eh4oVxAVfKG1Y14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Neurons are biologically immortal,  a mouse neuron transplanted into a rat lives twice as long as a mouse, and it is believed would potentially live indefinitely in even longer lived organism.",

      "author_id": "UCucqd0Q8S1cibjXurG_Q6kg",
      "author": "@diamond_s",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m12INDxrehfzOzq9xofITYAuYy19N2eCjpk5y_Rbnv8Q=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "but don't forget still in neurons there is a toxic accumulations so ultimately they are dying unfortunately",

      "text": "Can’t believe I’m commenting at 00:17 in, but if the goal of evolution is to survive, reproduce and adapt — then evolution has spent a loooooooooong time trying to extend our windows of time on all of those. Excited to actually get to that point in the conversation to be proved wrong lol.",

      "author_id": "UCtO5_E7iKfPfW1G4luj6FkA",
      "author": "@MichaelKleyn",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nWBkhs3XZcENi1MSPCdcXzpUjnMm2sZJbVobSifX-nvmmNb8bXfpOmj_RTnLGbL03qbA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgwyHJ4wwjXxA4OyAkl4AaABAg.AM6hZalrNyiAMBGn8fBDST",
      "parent": "UgwyHJ4wwjXxA4OyAkl4AaABAg",
      "text": "There is no \"goal\" of evolution, that's your first hint. Whatever survives survives because it is good enough to reproduce, and have its offspring good enough to reproduce, ad infinitum. See, flies only live for a month or so. Lobsters, on the other hand, don't age the way we do.",

      "author_id": "UCkWKw-mYG7wtGRGkAOcR_nQ",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n-rhioly44N4XO5GmhOzq9oDPL6UfvCYBDmHyKPC2NOqJo=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgwyHJ4wwjXxA4OyAkl4AaABAg",
      "text": "Ok, I watched until 00:19 and from the top of my head can say that for evolution the only thing that would matter is to have max(alive_offspring_that_can_repeoduce_too) so longevity is helpful, but not paramount (i.e. not on the level of having good immune system, or good eyesight, or whatever). But maybe someone even wiser and deeper into the video would come and prove me wrong.",

      "author_id": "UCPgWlgFBo05OmaL2eZGv_pQ",
      "author": "@RuslanLagashkin",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mbNny_cF51z2lx-L4RtwBzVzVzxEDm8HJrMilmPyMLLt8=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {

      "parent": "UgwyHJ4wwjXxA4OyAkl4AaABAg.AM6hZalrNyiAMIX_AOO0dy",
      "text": "​ @RuslanLagashkin  I would pretty much agree. \n\nAdding that even if an organism did max out longevity stats it would lead to it's higher death competitors to eventually out-compete or extinct the species.\n\nJust thought experiment wise if an individual could survive a ridiculous lifetime let's say thousands of years the species wouldn't need to rapidly reproduce (otherwise it would resource starve eventually) or a highly mutative virus evolves and wipes out the species before it can adapt or environmental changes say no e.g. a change in temperature, meteoroid impact, loss of habitat from another species.",

      "author_id": "UCsz1LPqMnf7LG4bzIRCOf6g",

      "id": "UgwXQhtM14yRcj94b9F4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Another possibility why evolution didn't push too hard on maximising aging. If hunters live for longer their population get larger. And this means that prey will diminish more quickly. The classic hunter-prey population curves would have more variance and if really pushed, that means that prey could even go locally extinct, triggering extinction of local hunters as well. So even if longevity mutations are easy to establish given bio-molecular constraints, local populations could go extinct and that's why we don't see many animals living for super long.",
      "like_count": 4,
      "author_id": "UCgckNS1H2QqdO-QmXX2vIfw",
      "author": "@Neomadra",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l1rjmJB6sUM5AoSxMTcIxmdlh70yA1dkKdL5-TudniYA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "7 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1758240000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwXQhtM14yRcj94b9F4AaABAg.AM627kWIQ3xAM6gK7FqiuR",
      "parent": "UgwXQhtM14yRcj94b9F4AaABAg",
      "text": "Animals like the Galapagos tortoise and saltwater crocodile live so long possibly because very few survive into adulthood, and then once they do, they have plenty of resources and a very slow metabolism. So they have very low fertility and mortality rates and therefore no incentive to die to make way for new generations. The same goes for certain species of whales and sharks except that they have very low fertility, period, without losing their young to predators.",

      "author_id": "UC86BvoLf12NzQAxJK6TaK1Q",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I don't think evolution hard-coded organisms to die, it probably just doesn't develop the functions needed for long life.       "text": " @GustavoRocha1  Not necessarily, the prey would also likely evolve in an arms race to be more evasive or defensive effectively capping the reproduction rate and the 'immortal' predators would only compete with each other and more aggressive, cannibalistic offspring could out compete or kill their parents/elders to maintain access to the resource of prey available to them in times of a predator/prey imbalance at least hypothetically.       "text": "Would be great to have Michael Levin on your podcast.",

      "author_id": "UC4vj_C7_EA6Efk3-ivk0PYw",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m2qIcQn0Qk_hfK4bZ6ChEsPGorL9sM3FwFmRqhIK2GZmwVmcJVrkwSIzi_j4UxJXPAHA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyvF6GKpSepFMiyRC14AaABAg.AM5d0lKeq_8AM5lV9yHfva",
      "parent": "UgyvF6GKpSepFMiyRC14AaABAg",
      "text": "Seconded - that would be awesome.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCIHFqv5bab9bce67tewVeAg",
      "author": "@rainshine2",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/83rLCMO_-Z28ocVUFJUJnEoUlr0kgdMTNvIEbaoIk7svyxZHpjZbdArL84yro3y1Lyu1xlLa=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyvF6GKpSepFMiyRC14AaABAg.AM5d0lKeq_8AM8aZdd1fyi",
      "parent": "UgyvF6GKpSepFMiyRC14AaABAg",
      "text": "Michael Levin is amongst that group of people like David Sinclair who overhype their science, and it takes a very educated, experienced person to be able to fact-check them. For example I really didn't like Dwarkesh's interview with George Church. It was good for the most part but George Church was quite hand-wavey with certain statements (like the mirror life thing), and Dwarkesh just doesn't have the field expertise to catch those and ask follow-up questions. I don't think Michael Levin is as snake-oily as David Sinclair but it's not as though he holds the entire answer to regeneration in his hands. I believe some of his \"bioelectricity\" findings are just rehashing the abilities of classical yamanaka factors / other transcription factors.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCB5rfTeMEwXL2FwGh4zgvsA",
      "author": "@fireglory23",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_k0OFG1CXzYf9WEicS13kI4GYgmGxI_k0GH-LgkENEerQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "7 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1758240000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyvF6GKpSepFMiyRC14AaABAg.AM5d0lKeq_8AM9A1tyLM79",
      "parent": "UgyvF6GKpSepFMiyRC14AaABAg.AM5d0lKeq_8AM8aZdd1fyi",
      "text": " @fireglory23 I will gladly admit that I know basically nothing about biology, but to me his work seems very impressive, even if he’s drawing upon Platonist metaphysics. As far as I understand it’s not just Yamanaka factors, it’s not sufficient to explain all their results. But I’d gladly listen to a conversation between him and a more mainstream biologist.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC4vj_C7_EA6Efk3-ivk0PYw",
      "author": "@fellowmartian-n2f",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m2qIcQn0Qk_hfK4bZ6ChEsPGorL9sM3FwFmRqhIK2GZmwVmcJVrkwSIzi_j4UxJXPAHA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "7 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1758240000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyvF6GKpSepFMiyRC14AaABAg.AM5d0lKeq_8AMAnOdQTBL1",
      "parent": "UgyvF6GKpSepFMiyRC14AaABAg.AM5d0lKeq_8AM9A1tyLM79",
      "text": "​​ @fellowmartian-n2f ​I should probably grant him more credit than how I made it seem in my previous comment - I think he's a very talented science communicator and he does have an interesting vision of manipulating bioelectricity, but ultimately bioelectrical signaling is another dartboard for us to aim at to change what transcription factors do. This is pretty easy to do in simple models like planaria (which is what Michael has done his research on) but it's a far cry from a realistically deliverable treatment on humans. I believe he is immersing planaria in small molecule drugs that target ion channels - that's not something you could do today to target a patient's liver or arm. Probably the other problem is that he keeps getting sensationalized by under-researched podcasters. The lex fridman one is really awful",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCB5rfTeMEwXL2FwGh4zgvsA",
      "author": "@fireglory23",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_k0OFG1CXzYf9WEicS13kI4GYgmGxI_k0GH-LgkENEerQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "There seems to be a simpler way to state KImmel's \"kin selection\" argument against longevity being adaptive: When times get tough it would seem advantageous to have parents that are NOT competing with you for resources.     {
      "id": "UgzcmC27IbECuavWK394AaABAg.AM5_MisDCUAAMhdV5fgQ4k",
      "parent": "UgzcmC27IbECuavWK394AaABAg",
      "text": "it's definitely simpler but your explanation wouldn't explain why anything other than microbial life evolved, no? Also his specific way of explaining it is from a human-centric standpoint e.g. humans evolved intelligence to fill an ecological niche which has drawbacks like the adolescent phase but the 'old' humans being alive can pass on knowledge to increase survival (therefore procreation chance) even in hard times. But there are diminishing returns when these 'old' humans don't meaningfully contribute to their kin in respect to their caloric intake so there is no evolution pressure to increase lifespan. \n\nAlso it is worth considering that aging is inherent from cell damage accumulated due to radiation, oxidative stress etc. so naturally metabolic intake increases with age because of the lower conversion efficiency and the evolutionary cost to fix this is higher than decreasing infant mortality, increasing reproduction amounts or other higher efficiency methods and evolution follows the path of least resistance because a high cost adaptation to reduce aging would cause more initial decreases in population growth relative to other means of adaption. This would theoretically mean that even if an organism happened to hit an insane lottery roll on mutation which led to it living longer it would be out-competed by the more efficient version of the same species or it could die faster than other hardier short life span versions in high hazard environments which responded to the evolutionary pressures more appropriately.\n\nThis concept is explained by Richard Dawkins when he references the recurrent laryngeal nerve which starts from the vagus nerve (brain stem) loops around the aorta and then heads back up to the larynx (inefficient) path but comes from the common ancestor of fish where the path didn't matter, despite this being incredibly inefficient in larger organisms especially in animals like giraffes the nerve still follows the same path because the evolutionary cost of simply extending the length of the nerve outweighs the fatal consequences of evolution trying to fix this otherwise inconsequential issue (in terms of gene replication).",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCsz1LPqMnf7LG4bzIRCOf6g",
      "author": "@nothinggood2696",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m020QLVo-Z2qNT4c7qKkozpEcPMmGdZdfctJ2Vj2A=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "is_pinned": false

## Description

Jacob Kimmel thinks he can find the transcription factors to reverse aging. We do a deep dive on why this might be plausible and why evolution hasn’t already optimized for longevity. We also talk about why drug discovery has been getting exponentially harder, and what a new platform for biological understanding to speed up progress would look like. As a bonus, we get into the nitty gritty of gene delivery and Jacob’s controversial takes on CAR-T cells. For full disclosure, I am an angel investor in NewLimit. This did not impact my decision to interview Jacob, nor the questions I asked him.

just a few cells in that dish, like a countable&nbsp; number on your fingers, would actually reprogram.&nbsp; But they would proliferate like mad. They form&nbsp; these big colonies. It's a single cell that&nbsp;&nbsp; just proliferates and forms a bunch of copies of&nbsp;

you randomly modify them, and then you compute&nbsp; a gradient on your parameters against your loss,&nbsp;&nbsp; and so you can take a gradient in that space. That's how I imagine evolution is working.&nbsp; So you need lots of those little edits to actually&nbsp;

that and certainly even worse at activating it.&nbsp; Small molecules can get all&nbsp; the way into the nucleus,&nbsp;&nbsp; but they can't do much once they're there.&nbsp; They're just too small. The other classic&nbsp;&nbsp;

in your normal genome, and that's why it's hard&nbsp;&nbsp; for the immune system to surveil it. Interesting. Interesting. It's funny&nbsp;&nbsp; that whenever we're trying to cure infectious&nbsp; diseases, we just have to deal with, "Fuck,&nbsp;&nbsp;

viruses have been evolving for billions of years&nbsp; with our oldest common ancestor, and they know&nbsp;&nbsp; exactly what they're doing, and it's so hard." Then whenever we're trying to do something else,&nbsp;&nbsp; we're like, "Fuck, the immune system has been&nbsp;

evolving for billions of years, and it knows&nbsp;&nbsp; what it's doing, and how do we get past it?" The Red Queen race is quite sophisticated.&nbsp; If you want to just throw a new&nbsp; tool into biology, you somehow have&nbsp;&nbsp;

to get around one side of that equation. Given the fact that it's somewhere between&nbsp;&nbsp; impossible and very far away but it's necessary&nbsp; for full curing of aging, does that mean that in&nbsp;&nbsp; the short run, in the next few decades, we'll&nbsp;

have some parts of our body which will have&nbsp;&nbsp; these amazing therapies, and then other parts&nbsp; which will just be stuck the way they are?&nbsp; You mentioned hepatocytes are some of the&nbsp; cells that you're able to actually study in&nbsp;&nbsp;

or deliver to. These are our liver cells. So&nbsp; you're saying, "Look, I can get drunk as much&nbsp;&nbsp; as I want and it's not going to have an impact on&nbsp; my long-run liver health because then you'll just&nbsp;&nbsp; inject me with this therapy."

But for the rest of my body,&nbsp;&nbsp; it's going to age as normal? What is the implication of the&nbsp;&nbsp; fact that the delivery seems to be lagging&nbsp; much behind your understanding of aging?&nbsp;

Just to give the delivery folks&nbsp; credit, they're currently ahead.&nbsp; There are currently no reprogramming&nbsp; medicines for aging, and there are&nbsp;&nbsp; medicines that deliver nucleic acids.

They're still winning the race against&nbsp;&nbsp; us right now, but to your point, I hope the&nbsp; lines cross. I hope we outcompete them. Even&nbsp;&nbsp; if you were able to only target some subsets of&nbsp; cells, it's not that you would see this strange,&nbsp;&nbsp;

Frankensteinian benefit in health in some&nbsp; aspects and lack of benefit entirely in others.&nbsp; What we've found across the history&nbsp; of medicine is that the body's an&nbsp;&nbsp; incredibly interconnected, complex system.

If you're able to rescue function even in&nbsp;&nbsp; one cell type in one tissue, you often&nbsp; have knock-on benefits in many places&nbsp;&nbsp; that you didn't initially anticipate. One way we can get examples of this&nbsp;&nbsp;

is through transplant experiments. Both in bone marrow and in liver,&nbsp;&nbsp; for example, we have fairly common&nbsp; transplant procedures that occur in humans.&nbsp; We can compare old humans who get livers&nbsp;

from young people or old people and ask a&nbsp;&nbsp; pretty controlled question. What occurs as a function&nbsp;&nbsp; of just having a young liver? Is it that, for example, you can eat a&nbsp;&nbsp;

lot of fatty food and drink a lot and be fine? Or is it that you see broader benefits?&nbsp; The latter seems to be true. They have reduced risk of&nbsp;&nbsp; several other diseases and overall better&nbsp;

survival as a function of having a younger&nbsp;&nbsp; liver than they do for an older one. Suggesting that because these tissues&nbsp;&nbsp; are so interconnected, many of&nbsp; these organs like the liver,&nbsp;&nbsp;

like your adipose tissue, are endocrine organs. They're also sending out signals to many other&nbsp;&nbsp; places in your body, helping coordinate&nbsp; your health across multiple tissue systems.&nbsp; Even just one tissue can benefit other tissue&nbsp;

systems in your body at the same time. HSCs are&nbsp;&nbsp; another example. These are mostly examples taken&nbsp; from a wonderful book by Frederick Appelbaum,&nbsp;&nbsp; who trained with Don Thomas, the physician&nbsp; who invented human bone marrow transplants.&nbsp;

There are many circumstances where patients&nbsp; got a bone marrow transplant and actually&nbsp;&nbsp; cured another disease they had as a result,&nbsp; maybe unanticipated, where it's even just the&nbsp;&nbsp; replacement of this one special cell type, HSCs,&nbsp;

that has knock-on effects throughout the body.&nbsp; There were symptoms of these diseases that&nbsp; presented in myriad ways throughout their&nbsp;&nbsp; system, but ultimately, its root&nbsp; cause was even just a single cell.&nbsp;

There are counterexamples as well where you&nbsp; can go into animals and break even just one&nbsp;&nbsp; gene in one specific subset of T cells. You can break a gene in there that encodes&nbsp;&nbsp; for a transcription factor in their&nbsp;

mitochondria called TFAM, and you&nbsp;&nbsp; dramatically shorten the lifespan of mice. One gene in one special type of T cells&nbsp;&nbsp; can give you that type of pathology. So it implies the inverse may also exist.&nbsp;

and your endocrine system coordinates a lot&nbsp;&nbsp; of the complex interplay between your tissues. I don't think the story is fully written yet&nbsp;&nbsp; on exactly why GLP-1 and GIP-1, broadly&nbsp; incretin mimetic medicines like Ozempic,&nbsp;&nbsp;

have so many knock-on benefits, but&nbsp; they're a great example of this phenomenon.&nbsp; If someone told you, "I'm going to find a&nbsp; single molecule, and I'm going to drug it,&nbsp;&nbsp; and it's not only going to have benefits for&nbsp;

decades of healthy life to individuals&nbsp; by reprogramming the age of individual&nbsp;&nbsp; cell types and individual tissues. How big will the payload have to be?&nbsp; How many transcription factors? I&nbsp;

Already in the clinic today, there are medicines&nbsp; that deliver many different genes as RNA.&nbsp; There are medicines where, for instance, it's&nbsp; a vaccine as a combination of flu and COVID&nbsp;&nbsp; proteins, and they're delivering 20 different&nbsp;

unique transcripts all at the same time.&nbsp; When you think about that already as a&nbsp; medicine that's being injected into people&nbsp;&nbsp; in trials, the idea of delivering just a few&nbsp; transcription factors is seemingly quotidian.&nbsp;

The expression level of transcription&nbsp;&nbsp; factors in your genome relative&nbsp; to other genes is incredibly low.&nbsp; If you just look at the rank-ordered list of what&nbsp; are the most frequently expressed genes in the&nbsp;&nbsp;

genome by the count of how many mRNAs are in the&nbsp; cell, transcription factors are near the bottom.&nbsp; That means you don't actually need to get&nbsp; that many copies of a transcription factor&nbsp;&nbsp; into a cell in order to have benefits.

What we've seen so far, and what I&nbsp;&nbsp; imagine will continue to play out, is that&nbsp; even fairly low doses of these medicines,&nbsp;&nbsp; which are well within the realm of what folks&nbsp; have been taking for more than a decade.&nbsp;

They are able to induce really strong efficacy. We're hopeful that not only will the actual size&nbsp;&nbsp; of the payload in terms of number&nbsp; of base pairs not be limiting,&nbsp;&nbsp; but the dose shouldn't be limiting either.

Would it have to be a chronic treatment,&nbsp;&nbsp; or could it just be a one-time dose? In principle, it could be one time.&nbsp; I think that would be an overstatement for today. I can talk you through the evidence from the&nbsp;&nbsp;

first principles back to the reality of&nbsp; what's the hardest thing we have in hand.&nbsp; Epigenetic reprogramming is basically how the&nbsp; cell types in our bodies right now are able&nbsp;&nbsp; to adopt the identities that they have.

of years if you want to take the example of a&nbsp; bowhead whale which uses the same mechanism.&nbsp; We also know that with very targeted edits,&nbsp; other groups have done this, folks like Luke&nbsp;&nbsp; Gilbert now at the Arc Institute, who I think of&nbsp;

as one of the great unsung scientists of our time,&nbsp;&nbsp; have been able to make a targeted edit in&nbsp; a single locus and then show that you can&nbsp;&nbsp; actually make cells divide 400-plus times over&nbsp; multiple years in an incubator in the lab.&nbsp;

Luke developed in his lab in monkeys&nbsp;&nbsp; and shown they last at least a couple of years. In principle, the upper bound here is really long.&nbsp; You could potentially have one dose and it&nbsp; lasts a very long time, potentially decades, as&nbsp;&nbsp;

long as it took you to age the first time maybe. We don't have data like that today. I don't want&nbsp;&nbsp; to overstate. We do have data that these positive&nbsp; effects can last several weeks after a dose.&nbsp; You could imagine, even without many leaps&nbsp;

of faith up toward this upper bound limit&nbsp;&nbsp; of what's possible just from the data we have in&nbsp; hand now, that you could get doses every month,&nbsp;&nbsp; every few months and actually have really&nbsp; dramatic benefits that persist over time,&nbsp;&nbsp;

rather than needing to get an IV every&nbsp; day, which might not be tractable.&nbsp; We've got 1600 transcription&nbsp; factors in the human genome.&nbsp; Is it worth looking at non-human TFs&nbsp;

and seeing what effects they might have,&nbsp;&nbsp; or are they unlikely to be the right search space? I think it's less likely. I think you have a prior&nbsp;&nbsp; that evolution has given you a reasonable&nbsp; basis set for navigating the states that&nbsp;&nbsp;

human cells might want to occupy. In our case, we know that the state&nbsp;&nbsp; we're trying to access is encoded&nbsp; by some combination of these TFs.&nbsp; It does arise in development obviously.

We're trying to make an old cell look young,&nbsp;&nbsp; not look like some Frankenstein&nbsp; cell that's never been seen before.&nbsp; That said, we don't have any guarantees that the&nbsp; way aging progresses is by following the same&nbsp;&nbsp;

basis set of these transcription factor programs&nbsp; in the genome that are encoded during development.&nbsp; I don't think it's unreasonable to ask, "Would&nbsp; your eventual ideal reprogramming medicine&nbsp;&nbsp; necessarily be a composition of the natural TFs,&nbsp;

or would it include something like TFs from other&nbsp;&nbsp; organisms, as you posit, or even entirely&nbsp; synthetic transcription factors as well?"&nbsp;&nbsp; Things like Super-SOX. Super-SOX is&nbsp; a particular publication from Sergiy&nbsp;&nbsp;

Velychko where they mutated the SOX2 gene and&nbsp; they made more efficient iPSC reprogramming.&nbsp; They could take somatic cells and turn them&nbsp; into pluripotent stem cells more effectively&nbsp;&nbsp; than you could with just the canonical Yamanaka&nbsp;

factors, which are Oct-4, Sox2, KLF4, and Myc.&nbsp; iPSC reprogramming never happens in nature,&nbsp; so there's no reason to necessarily believe&nbsp;&nbsp; that the natural TFs are optimal. So even really simple optimizations,&nbsp;&nbsp;

like just mutagenizing one of the four&nbsp; Yamanaka factors we already know about&nbsp;&nbsp; or swapping some domains between a few&nbsp; TFs, seem to improve things dramatically.&nbsp; I think that's a pretty good signal that&nbsp;

actually there's a lot of gradient to climb&nbsp;&nbsp; here and that potentially for us, the end-state&nbsp; products we're developing in 2100 are more like&nbsp;&nbsp; synthetic genes that have never existed, rather&nbsp; than just compositions of the natural set.&nbsp;

What about the effects of aging? Your skin starts to sag because of the&nbsp;&nbsp; effects of gravity over the course of decades? Is&nbsp; that a cellular process? How would some cellular&nbsp;&nbsp; therapy deal with that?

The best evidence is&nbsp;&nbsp; that it's probably not cellular. The reason your skin sags is there's a protein&nbsp;&nbsp; in your skin called elastin, which does exactly&nbsp; what you'd think it would based on the name.&nbsp;

It kind of keeps your skin elastic-y, like&nbsp; a waistband, and holds it to your face.&nbsp; You have these big polymerized&nbsp; fibers of elastin in your face.&nbsp; As far as we understand it, you only polymerize&nbsp;

it and form a long fiber during development.&nbsp; Then the rest of your life, you make&nbsp; the individual units of the polymer,&nbsp;&nbsp; but for reasons no one as far as I can&nbsp; tell understands, they fail to polymerize.&nbsp;

You can't make new long cords to&nbsp; hold your skin up to your face.&nbsp; So the eventual solution for something like&nbsp; that is likely that you need to program cells&nbsp;&nbsp; to states that are extra-physiological.

There might not be a cell in your body.&nbsp; It's not just like a young skin cell from a&nbsp; 20-year-old is better at making these fibers.&nbsp; As far as we can tell, they don't. But you could probably program a cell to&nbsp;&nbsp;

be able to reinvigorate that polymerization&nbsp; process, to run along the fiber and repair&nbsp;&nbsp; it in places where it's damaged. Obviously these things get made&nbsp;&nbsp; during development, so it's totally&nbsp;

physically feasible for this to occur.&nbsp; Maybe there's even a developmental&nbsp; state which would be sufficient to&nbsp;&nbsp; achieve this. I don't think anyone knows. But&nbsp; that would be the kind of state that one might&nbsp;&nbsp;

have to engineer de novo, even if our genome&nbsp; doesn't necessarily encode for it explicitly.&nbsp; Interesting. Okay, what is Eroom's Law? Eroom's Law is a funny portmanteau created&nbsp;&nbsp; by a friend of mine, Jack Scannell.

He inverted the notion of Moore's Law,&nbsp;&nbsp; which is the doubling of compute density&nbsp; on silicon chips every few years.&nbsp; Moore's Law has graciously given&nbsp; us massive increases in compute&nbsp;&nbsp;

performance over several decades. Eroom's Law is the inverse of that.&nbsp; In biopharma, what we're actually seeing&nbsp; is that there's a very consistent decrease&nbsp;&nbsp; in the number of new molecular entities,&nbsp;

new medicines that we're able to invent,&nbsp;&nbsp; per billion dollars invested. This trend actually starts way&nbsp;&nbsp; back in the 1950s and persists through many&nbsp; different technological transitions along the way.&nbsp;

It seems to be an incredibly consistent&nbsp; feature of trying to make new medicines.&nbsp; In a weird way, Eroom's Law is actually&nbsp; very similar to the scaling laws you&nbsp;&nbsp; have in ML, where you have this very&nbsp;

consistent logarithmic relationship.&nbsp; You throw in more inputs and you get&nbsp; consistently diminishing outputs.&nbsp; The difference, of course, is that this trend&nbsp; in ML has been used to raise exponentially more&nbsp;&nbsp;

investment and to drive more hype towards AI. Whereas in biotech, modulo NewLimit's new round,&nbsp;&nbsp; it has driven down valuations,&nbsp; driven down excitement and energy.&nbsp; With AI at least you can internalize the extra&nbsp;

cost and the extra benefits because there's&nbsp;&nbsp; this general purpose model you're training. This year you spend $100 million training&nbsp;&nbsp; a model, next year $1 billion,&nbsp; the year after that, $10 billion.&nbsp;

But it's one general purpose model, unlike, "We&nbsp; made money on this drug and now we're going to&nbsp;&nbsp; use that money to invest in 10 different&nbsp; drugs in 10 different bespoke ways."&nbsp; I was gearing up to ask you, what would a general&nbsp;

purpose platform—where even if you had diminishing&nbsp;&nbsp; returns, at least you can have this less bespoke&nbsp; way of designing drugs—look like for biotech?&nbsp; I'm going to slightly dodge your question&nbsp; first to maybe analyze something really&nbsp;&nbsp;

interesting that you highlighted. You have these two phenomena:&nbsp;&nbsp; ML scaling and then scaling in terms&nbsp; of the cost for new drug discovery.&nbsp; Why is it that the patterns of&nbsp;

investment have been so different?&nbsp; There are probably two key features&nbsp; that might explain this difference.&nbsp; One is that the returns to the scaled&nbsp; output in the case of ML actually are&nbsp;&nbsp;

expected to increase super exponentially. If you actually reach AGI, it's going to be a much&nbsp;&nbsp; larger value than just even a few logs back on&nbsp; the performance curve that people are following.&nbsp; Whereas in the life sciences thus&nbsp;

far, each of those products we're&nbsp;&nbsp; generating further and further out on the&nbsp; Eroom's Law curve as time moves forward,&nbsp;&nbsp; haven't necessarily scaled in their potential&nbsp; revenue and their potential returns quite so much.&nbsp;

You're seeing these increased costs&nbsp; not counterbalanced by increased ROI.&nbsp; The other piece of it that you highlighted is&nbsp; that it’s unlike building a general model where&nbsp;&nbsp; potentially by making larger investments, you can&nbsp;

be able to solve a broader addressable market,&nbsp;&nbsp; moving from solving very narrow&nbsp; tasks to eventually replacing large&nbsp;&nbsp; fractions of white collar intelligence. In biotech, when you're traditionally&nbsp;&nbsp;

able to develop a medicine in a given&nbsp; indication—"I was able to treat disease&nbsp;&nbsp; X"—it doesn't necessarily engender you to be&nbsp; able to then treat "disease Y" more readily.&nbsp; Typically where these biotech firms in general&nbsp;

have been able to develop unique expertise is on&nbsp;&nbsp; making molecules to target particular genes,&nbsp; so "I'm really good at making a molecule&nbsp;&nbsp; that intervenes on gene X or gene Y." It turns out that the ability to make&nbsp;&nbsp;

those molecules more rapidly isn't actually&nbsp; reducing the largest risk in the process.&nbsp; This means that the ability to go from&nbsp; one or two outputs one year to then&nbsp;&nbsp; four the next is much more limited.

This brings us then to the question&nbsp;&nbsp; of what the general model would be in biology. I think it reduces down to how do you actually&nbsp;&nbsp; imbue those two properties that create the ML&nbsp; scaling law curve of hope and bring those over&nbsp;&nbsp;

to biology so that you can take the Eroom's&nbsp; law curve and potentially give it the same&nbsp;&nbsp; sort of potential beneficial spin. There are a few different versions&nbsp;&nbsp; of this you could imagine.

But I'll address the first point.&nbsp; How do you get to a place where you're&nbsp; actually able to generate more revenue per&nbsp;&nbsp; medicine so that potentially the outputs&nbsp; you're generating are more valuable,&nbsp;&nbsp;

even if each output might cost a bit more? Traditionally, when we've developed medicines,&nbsp;&nbsp; we go after fairly narrow indications, meaning&nbsp; diseases that fairly small numbers of people get.&nbsp; That's actually increased, in terms of the&nbsp;

narrow scope of what medicines are addressing,&nbsp;&nbsp; as we've gone forward in time. This is sort of an ironic situation&nbsp;&nbsp; where we've gone from addressing pretty broad&nbsp; categories of disease, like infectious disease,&nbsp;&nbsp;

to narrower and narrower genetically-defined&nbsp; diseases that have small patient populations.&nbsp; Because these only affect a few people—if you&nbsp; think about the value function of a medicine as&nbsp;&nbsp; how many years of healthy life it gives how many&nbsp;

people—if the "how many people" is pretty small,&nbsp;&nbsp; it just really bounds the amount&nbsp; of value you're able to generate.&nbsp; You need to then be able to find&nbsp; medicines that treat most people.&nbsp;

All of us will one day get sick and die. So arguably, the TAM for any really successful&nbsp;&nbsp; medicine could be everybody on planet Earth. We need to find a way to be able to route&nbsp;&nbsp; toward medicines that address&nbsp;

these very large populations.&nbsp; The second piece then is, how do we&nbsp; actually build models that enable us&nbsp;&nbsp; to take the success in one medicine we've&nbsp; developed and lead that to an increased&nbsp;&nbsp;

really the hard part of drug discovery.&nbsp; Figuring out what to make an antibody to&nbsp; target is the hard thing about drug discovery.&nbsp; What gene do I intervene upon in order to&nbsp; actually treat a disease in a given patient?&nbsp;

claim that we know how to engage with&nbsp; the right hook, we just don't know&nbsp;&nbsp; what that hook is supposed to do in the body. I don't know if that's the way you describe it.&nbsp; Another claim that I've seen is that with small&nbsp;

way of explaining this–if you were to write&nbsp; out a list of well-known targets that many,&nbsp;&nbsp; many folks would agree are the correct genes to&nbsp; go after and to try and inhibit or activate in&nbsp;&nbsp; order to treat a given set of diseases—and&nbsp;

the only reason we don't have medicines is&nbsp;&nbsp; that we can't figure out a trick in order to&nbsp; be able to drug them—it's a fairly small list.&nbsp; It would probably fit on a single page. Whereas the number of possible indications&nbsp;&nbsp;

that one could go after, and the number&nbsp; of possible genes that one could intervene&nbsp;&nbsp; upon especially when you consider&nbsp; their combinations, is astronomical.&nbsp; The experiment you could run here is if you&nbsp;

lock 10 really smart drug developers in a room.&nbsp; You tell them to write down some incredibly&nbsp; high-conviction target disease pairs where&nbsp;&nbsp; they're sure if they modulate this biology,&nbsp; these patients are going to benefit.&nbsp;

You can actually look for this.&nbsp; There are some existence proofs you&nbsp; can look for out in the universe.&nbsp; If the only problem was that we didn't have&nbsp; the ability to drug something using current&nbsp;&nbsp;

therapeutics that we can put in humans, we&nbsp; should still be able to treat it in the best&nbsp;&nbsp; animal models of that disease because we&nbsp; can use things like transgenic systems.&nbsp; You can go in and you can engineer&nbsp;

the genome of that animal.&nbsp; This gives you all sorts of superpowers that&nbsp; you don't have in patients, but allow you to,&nbsp;&nbsp; for instance, turn on arbitrarily complex groups&nbsp; of genes in arbitrarily specific or broad groups&nbsp;&nbsp;

of cells in the organism, at any time you&nbsp; want, at any dose you want in the animal.&nbsp; For the majority of pathologies, we&nbsp; just don't have many of those examples.&nbsp; What is the answer to what is the general purpose&nbsp;

thing where every marginal discovery increases the&nbsp;&nbsp; odds you make the next discovery? There are multiple ways one might&nbsp;&nbsp; approach this problem. The most common today,&nbsp;&nbsp;

this is often what people are describing&nbsp; when they talk about a virtual cell.&nbsp; This is a very nebulous idea, sometimes numinous,&nbsp; if you'll let me describe it in that way as well.&nbsp; Concretely, what most people are trying&nbsp;

to do is measure some number of molecules,&nbsp;&nbsp; or perceived emissions like the morphology of&nbsp; a cell, and then perturb it many times, turn&nbsp;&nbsp; some genes on, turn some genes off, and measure&nbsp; how that molecular morphological state changes.&nbsp;

The notion is that there's a lot&nbsp; of mutual information in biology.&nbsp; If I measure something, most commonly all the&nbsp; genes the cell is using at a given moment,&nbsp;&nbsp; which you can get by RNA sequencing,&nbsp;

I get a decent enough picture of&nbsp;&nbsp; most of the other complexity going on. I can take a bunch of healthy cells and a bunch&nbsp;&nbsp; of cells that are in a diseased or aged state. I'm able then to compare those profiles and say,&nbsp;&nbsp;

"Okay, my diseased cells use these&nbsp; genes, my healthy cells use these.&nbsp; Are there any interventions that I'm&nbsp; able to experimentally find in the&nbsp;&nbsp; lab that shift one toward the other?"

The hope would be that, because you're&nbsp;&nbsp; never going to be able to scan combinatorially all&nbsp; the possible groups of genes to make it concrete.&nbsp; There's something like 20,000 genes in the genome. You can then choose however many&nbsp;&nbsp;

genes in your combination you want. It's not crazy to think of hundreds at a time.&nbsp;&nbsp; That's what transcription factors control. That's&nbsp; how development works. So the number of possible&nbsp;&nbsp; combinations is truly astronomical.

You just can't test it all.&nbsp; The hope would be that by doing some sparse&nbsp; sampling of those pairs—what your inputs are,&nbsp;&nbsp; here's what the cell looked like&nbsp; beforehand, here's the particular&nbsp;&nbsp;

genes I perturbed—you have some measurement&nbsp; then of the state that the cell resulted in.&nbsp; Here's which genes went&nbsp; up, here's which went down.&nbsp; Once I've trained a model to predict from&nbsp;

the perturbations to the output on the cell&nbsp;&nbsp; state, you can start to ask what would happen&nbsp; for some arbitrary combinations of genes.&nbsp; Now in silico I can search all possible&nbsp; things that one might do and potentially&nbsp;&nbsp;

discover targets that take my diseased&nbsp; cells back to something like healthy cells.&nbsp; So that's another version&nbsp; of what an all-encompassing&nbsp;&nbsp; model would look like where you actually&nbsp;

have compounding returns in drug discovery.&nbsp; You basically described one of the models&nbsp; you guys are working on at NewLimit.&nbsp; You're training this model based&nbsp; on this data where you're taking&nbsp;&nbsp;

the entire transcriptome and just labeling&nbsp; it based on how old that cell actually is.&nbsp; If you've got all this data you're collecting&nbsp; on how different perturbations are having&nbsp;&nbsp; different phenotypic effects on a&nbsp;

cell, why only record whether that&nbsp;&nbsp; effect correlates with more or less aging? Why can't you also label it with all the other&nbsp;&nbsp; effects that we might eventually care about&nbsp; and eventually get the full virtual cell?&nbsp;

That's a more general purpose model, not just the&nbsp; one that predicts whether a cell looks old or not.&nbsp; Absolutely, we actually do both today. We can train these models where the inputs&nbsp;&nbsp; are a notion of what that cell looked like at&nbsp;

the starting place, here's what a generic old&nbsp;&nbsp; cell looked like, and then representations&nbsp; of the transcription factors themselves.&nbsp; We derive those from protein foundation models. They're language models trained&nbsp;&nbsp;

on protein sequences. It turns out that gives you a&nbsp;&nbsp; really good base level understanding of biology. The model's starting from a pretty smart place.&nbsp; Then you can predict a number of different targets&nbsp;

from some learned embedding, the same way you&nbsp;&nbsp; could have multiple heads on a language model. One of those for us is actually just predicting&nbsp;&nbsp; every gene the cell is expressing. Can I just recapitulate the entire state&nbsp;&nbsp;

and guess what effect these transcription&nbsp; factors will have on every given gene?&nbsp; You can think about that as an objective&nbsp; rather than a value judgment on the cell.&nbsp; I'm not asking whether or not I&nbsp;

want this particular transcriptome.&nbsp; I'm just asking what it will look like. Then we also have something more like&nbsp;&nbsp; value judgments. I believe that that&nbsp;&nbsp;

transcriptome looks like a younger cell. I'm going to select on that and train ahead&nbsp;&nbsp; to predict it where I can denoise across&nbsp; genes and then select for younger cells.&nbsp; But you could do that for arbitrary&nbsp;

numbers of additional heads.&nbsp; What are some other states you might want? Do I want to polarize T cells to a less&nbsp;&nbsp; inflammatory state in somebody&nbsp; with an autoimmune disease?&nbsp;

Do I want to make liver cells more functional&nbsp; in a patient who's suffering from certain&nbsp;&nbsp; types of metabolic syndrome, maybe even&nbsp; orthogonal to the way that they age?&nbsp; Do I want to go in and change the way a neuron&nbsp;

is functioning to a different state to treat a&nbsp;&nbsp; particular type of neurodegenerative disease? These are all questions you can ask.&nbsp; They're not the ones we're going after, but&nbsp; that is the more general, broader vision.&nbsp;

cost disease, which is very unrelated to&nbsp;&nbsp; pharmaceutical discoveries but is something&nbsp; that we will have to solve in the system.&nbsp; Part of it's the disintermediation of the&nbsp; actual customer and the actual provider.&nbsp;

a lot of the types of administration costs. It’s not just administration like admins at&nbsp;&nbsp; hospitals, but the cost of administering existing&nbsp; medicines and therapies to you. That’s going down.&nbsp;&nbsp; One stat on why I think that's true.

that burden from the administration&nbsp; system to the pharmaceutical system.&nbsp; The pharmaceutical system is&nbsp; the only piece of healthcare&nbsp;&nbsp; where technology has made us more efficient.

### Comment 59
- comment_id: UgzdxQDF2HCBYBbUZ114AaABAg.AMDiEzOKZTOAMhjZ_RF_GW
- parent_id: UgzdxQDF2HCBYBbUZ114AaABAg
- author: @nothinggood2696
- author_id: UCsz1LPqMnf7LG4bzIRCOf6g
- published_at: 2025-09-19T00:00:00.000Z
- like_count: 0
- is_favorited: false
- author_is_uploader: false

> Yes and no, aging is more complex than just the shortening of telomeres and telomeres only shorten because they act as a cancer suppression system, if they didn't shorten the likelihood of cancer would increase dramatically and immune systems and cells would still weaken with age from cell replication errors, cell damage from radiation/oxidative stress, immune compromises etc. so a species of organism without the shortening would likely die out very fast. Red blood cells don't reproduce (They are produced from stem cells) and die after around 120 days this is because they are terminally differentiated to maximize the surface area (oxygen transportation) capabilities, if these cells didn't die they would circulate around the body and become damaged to the point of anemia and would starve organs from their oxygen supply and you would die.
> 
> This isn't exactly accurate because red blood cells are recycled by phagocytes which recycle the damaged/dead blood cells rather telomere shortening but again imagine if the vast majority of these phagocytes in the body were cancerous/unable to perform this function and the consequences are the same.
> 
> In short, telomeres that shorten paradoxically extend the life of organisms like mammals across the species because high turnover cells don't become cancerous and kill you. Also I don't think self-repairing is possible without cell death ironically for the same reasons. It's like how to clean something you have to make something else dirty or in this case for the organism to stay alive cells have to die.

> Another possibility why evolution didn't push too hard on maximising aging. If hunters live for longer their population get larger. And this means that prey will diminish more quickly. The classic hunter-prey population curves would have more variance and if really pushed, that means that prey could even go locally extinct, triggering extinction of local hunters as well. So even if longevity mutations are easy to establish given bio-molecular constraints, local populations could go extinct and that's why we don't see many animals living for super long.

> ​​ @fellowmartian-n2f ​I should probably grant him more credit than how I made it seem in my previous comment - I think he's a very talented science communicator and he does have an interesting vision of manipulating bioelectricity, but ultimately bioelectrical signaling is another dartboard for us to aim at to change what transcription factors do. This is pretty easy to do in simple models like planaria (which is what Michael has done his research on) but it's a far cry from a realistically deliverable treatment on humans. I believe he is immersing planaria in small molecule drugs that target ion channels - that's not something you could do today to target a patient's liver or arm. > it's definitely simpler but your explanation wouldn't explain why anything other than microbial life evolved, no? Also his specific way of explaining it is from a human-centric standpoint e.g. humans evolved intelligence to fill an ecological niche which has drawbacks like the adolescent phase but the 'old' humans being alive can pass on knowledge to increase survival (therefore procreation chance) even in hard times. But there are diminishing returns when these 'old' humans don't meaningfully contribute to their kin in respect to their caloric intake so there is no evolution pressure to increase lifespan. 
> 
> Also it is worth considering that aging is inherent from cell damage accumulated due to radiation, oxidative stress etc. so naturally metabolic intake increases with age because of the lower conversion efficiency and the evolutionary cost to fix this is higher than decreasing infant mortality, increasing reproduction amounts or other higher efficiency methods and evolution follows the path of least resistance because a high cost adaptation to reduce aging would cause more initial decreases in population growth relative to other means of adaption. This would theoretically mean that even if an organism happened to hit an insane lottery roll on mutation which led to it living longer it would be out-competed by the more efficient version of the same species or it could die faster than other hardier short life span versions in high hazard environments which responded to the evolutionary pressures more appropriately.
> 
> This concept is explained by Richard Dawkins when he references the recurrent laryngeal nerve which starts from the vagus nerve (brain stem) loops around the aorta and then heads back up to the larynx (inefficient) path but comes from the common ancestor of fish where the path didn't matter, despite this being incredibly inefficient in larger organisms especially in animals like giraffes the nerve still follows the same path because the evolutionary cost of simply extending the length of the nerve outweighs the fatal consequences of evolution trying to fix this otherwise inconsequential issue (in terms of gene replication).
